name: Brazilian integralism
summary: Brazilian Integralism is the doctrine of the Ação Integralista Brasileira (AIB), founded by Plínio Salgado in 1932 under the motto God, Fatherland and Family. It sought an Integral State that replaces liberal democracy and political parties with representation through professional classes, corporations, families and municipalities, harmonises capital and labour under state supervision, nationalises strategic services and spreads small property, rejecting both liberal capitalism and communism. It is spiritualist and Catholic in inspiration, defines the Brazilian nation as a fusion of all races to be culturally assimilated, and carried a strong antisemitic strand led by Gustavo Barroso.
scope: The AIB's doctrine from its founding in October 1932 to its dissolution under the Estado Novo (1937-38), as the defining scholarship presents it (Klein s17, Lesser s18, Gonçalves s2/s3, Moraes s4): the October 1932 Manifesto, the AIB's Statutes, Diretrizes and Cartilha, the 1936 Manifesto-Programa, and the 1930s writings of its three doctrinaires, Plínio Salgado, Miguel Reale and Gustavo Barroso. It excludes Salgado's postwar Partido de Representação Popular and the neo-integralist groups, and other countries' integralisms. The AIB never held state power, so the profile rests on its words.

sources.title: Manifesto de Outubro de 1932
sources.author: Plínio Salgado, Ação Integralista Brasileira (Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Founding document: God and the nation, class harmony, organisation by professional classes and indirect election, nationalism against cosmopolitanism and communism, property, family, municipality, the Integral State.

sources.title: Diretrizes Integralistas
sources.author: Ação Integralista Brasileira (Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Doctrinal guidelines: hierarchy of the spiritual over the national, individual subordinate to the community, indissoluble family, family wage and vote, education, state supervision of media, concordat, nationalisations, corporative vote, political centralisation. The archive's copy is a later edition (it cites the 1934 Constitution and mentions television).

sources.title: Estatutos da Ação Integralista Brasileira, art. 3 (1935)
sources.author: Ação Integralista Brasileira, II Congress, Petrópolis (Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Aims of the AIB: God, fatherland and family, national unity, order and authority, social justice, corporations, property limited by the common good, natural resources, armed forces, no struggles between races or classes.

sources.title: Cartilha do Integralismo Brasileiro (1933)
sources.author: Miguel Reale (rapporteur), with Plínio Salgado, João Leães Sobrinho and J. Canuto Mendes de Almeida; archive copy with Reale's 1936 revisions (Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Catechism of the doctrine: state above classes, corporative representation, no parties, unions under the state, labour courts, property and its dissemination, nationalisations, free medical care, schooling, control of press and cinema, against liberalism and bolshevism.

sources.title: Manifesto-Programa de 1936
sources.author: Plínio Salgado, Ação Integralista Brasileira (doctrinal sections; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: 1936 programme: freedom of conscience and concordat, corporations as the popular will, economic plans and distribution of property, armed forces, South American unity, judiciary, right and duty of work, arts and press.

sources.title: Estado Totalitário e Estado Integral
sources.author: Plínio Salgado (A Offensiva, 1 November 1936; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: The Integral State as a state of law that does not absorb person, family, economy or religion; doctrine on sedition and the use of force.

sources.title: Nacional-Socialismo e Nacionalismo Cristão
sources.author: Plínio Salgado (A Offensiva, 14 February 1936; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Salgado's rejection of Nazi racism, the deification of the Führer and sterilisation, and his Christian foundation for the movement.

sources.title: O Integralismo e os Judeus
sources.author: Miguel Reale (A Offensiva, 13 December 1934; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Reale's rejection of the racist thesis, the fusion of all ethnicities in Brazil, and his conditional stance toward Jews and 'international banking'.

sources.title: O que é o Integralismo
sources.author: Gustavo Barroso (O que o Integralista deve saber, 1935; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Barroso's account: doctrine not programme, corporative state, rejection of terrorism and sabotage, renunciation and simplicity, corruption of the regime, foreign loans, inner revolution, reason under God.

sources.title: O Estado Corporativo
sources.author: Gustavo Barroso (Espírito do Século XX, 1936; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Corporative state: unions as natural organs, capital, labour and technique in harmony, rejection of universal suffrage, municipal-provincial-national indirect election, Senate of intellectual professions.

sources.title: Como é a Revolução Integralista (O modus da Revolução)
sources.author: Gustavo Barroso (Espírito do Século XX, 1936; Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Revolution by doctrine and example, peaceful conquest, regeneration of individuals rather than laws.

sources.title: Carta Brasileira do Trabalho
sources.author: Gustavo Barroso, written at Plínio Salgado's order for the AIB Supreme Council (Frente Integralista Brasileira archive, Wayback copy)
sources.usedFor: Labour charter: property as natural right with duties, family, dignity of the person, harmony of capital and labour, right and duty of work, collective contracts, labour magistracy, just and family wage, planned economy.

sources.title: Our Brazil Will Awake! The Acção Integralista Brasileira and the Failed Quest for a Fascist Order in the 1930s
sources.author: Marcus Klein, Cuadernos del CEDLA (Amsterdam, 2004)
sources.usedFor: History and doctrine of the AIB: fascist identification, the Chefe Nacional's powers, the 1935 turn to legality, race and miscegenation, assimilation of immigrants, the campaign against Japanese immigration, antisemitism, women, minimum wage.

sources.title: Integralist Action (AIB)
sources.author: Jeffrey Lesser, Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (via Encyclopedia.com)
sources.usedFor: Reference definition: the AIB as Brazil's first national fascist movement, its motto, Salgado as leader and Barroso as chief ideologue; scope.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa promises to strengthen the armed forces, and the Statutes make their greatness and prestige an aim.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The Diretrizes ask for family law, the protected 'family property' and the family wage and vote, making marriage and the family a legal institution.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The Carta Brasileira do Trabalho and the Statutes keep wages, asking for a just and family wage fixed by collective contracts.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Barroso's Carta Brasileira do Trabalho makes employer and worker partners under collective contracts that fix wages, keeping wage labour within the corporative order.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The Carta Brasileira do Trabalho calls property a natural right prior and superior to the state, and the Cartilha wants property spread, not abolished.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Klein shows the Integralists identified with European fascism at their start, Salgado saying that only fascism could raise Brazil.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Klein shows that Reale demanded Portuguese schooling and the fusion of German-Brazilians into the national community, and the Manifesto praises immigrants whose descendants are integrated.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Under the Diretrizes the Integral State permits no political force outside its control that could threaten it, and abolishes parties altogether.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Diretrizes limit the arts by moral imperatives under state supervision, but the Manifesto-Programa says Integralism does not seek to impose an art and condemns every kind of government censorship, so the sources point both ways.

central-planning.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa has the state draw up plans for sectors of the economy, and Barroso's Carta Brasileira do Trabalho calls for a 'planned economy under the control of intelligence' in place of the free market.

civilizational-union.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa aims at the moral, cultural, political and economic unity of South America, with a permanent institute in which all its governments sit and a great continental unity of the Latin nations.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Manifesto says men and classes 'can and must live in harmony' and that the social question is solved by the cooperation of all, and Barroso makes capital and labour forces that complete each other.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The Cartilha calls class struggle a morbid phenomenon found only in the liberal state, and the Manifesto puts the harmony of classes, under a common supernatural end, at the root of society.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Cartilha says only the collective labour contract protects workers, since individual contracts leave them to the law of supply and demand, and the Manifesto has organised classes guarantee their members in collective contracts.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Salgado rejects Sorel's doctrine as Darwinian 'struggle for life', and the Cartilha opposes free competition as setting men against each other.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Manifesto says a government that comes from the free will of all classes represents the fatherland, and the Manifesto-Programa calls corporations the only organs able to express the popular will.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Barroso calls for simplicity of life and modesty of conduct, and the Carta says the economy exists for man and must not be the nation's only end.

corporate-influence.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto wants an authority able to stop 'the rich, the powerful, the foreigners' and political groups from influencing government decisions.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Cartilha has state-recognised unions of employers and of employees meet in corporations, organs of the state that settle wages and profits and set rules for production and distribution.

culture-before-state.rationale: The 1935 Statutes seek the reform of the state 'through the formation of a new philosophical and legal culture', and Barroso makes the inner, moral revolution the first one.

decide-locally.rationale: The Manifesto makes municipalities autonomous in their own interests, but the Diretrizes and Cartilha combine administrative decentralisation with political centralisation, so the doctrine points both ways.

defeat-communism.rationale: The Manifesto vows a campaign 'without truce against Russian communism', and the Cartilha announces a fight without truce against internationalist communism.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The Manifesto and Cartilha oppose the Soviet state as an exploiting caste and a single boss, and vow to fight Russian communism without truce.

democracy-best.rationale: The doctrine calls itself an organic democracy but rejects universal suffrage as 'the lie of universal suffrage' and the vote by number, so it does not accept the voters' choice as final.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Diretrizes reject 'democratismo' and want representation as a qualitative index of the nation, not a quantitative one, and the Cartilha calls universal suffrage a lie.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: The Manifesto's Integral State is to be free of every principle of division, parties, class struggle, regional factions and antagonisms between government and people.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The Cartilha says government can never be in the power of a class, and it condemns Bolshevism for making the state the single boss that enslaves the workers.

direct-action.rationale: The Manifesto calls its campaign cultural, moral and educational and in the open, and the Manifesto-Programa seeks power through the processes of the 1934 Constitution and electoral law.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The Cartilha has the presidents of the states and of the Union chosen indirectly by the corporative chambers and the Senate.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Klein shows that the Integralists saw the Brazilian nation as a product of miscegenation, and Reale calls Brazil the place where all ethnicities meet and fuse.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The Statutes tie pay both to the worker's needs and to his contribution to the national economy, and the Manifesto gives workers profits according to effort and capacity.

dominated-front.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa calls for the complete independence of the South American continent from outside influences and its solidarity against the international financiers.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Diretrizes declare every individual subordinate, within his sphere, to the superior interests of the community and insist on the duty to fulfil all social obligations.

elective-rulers.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto has the Head of the Nation elected by the national congresses of class representatives.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Carta calls the human person sacred in its dignity, and the Manifesto-Programa promises measures for 'the true equality of all Brazilians before the national state'.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Manifesto wants each person to rise according to vocation, aptitude and effort within a hierarchy, not equal results.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Manifesto creates the nation 'with all the racial elements' and attacks ethnic prejudices imported from abroad, and Reale calls Brazil the place where all ethnicities fuse.

experts-over-public.rationale: The Manifesto calls for the direct participation of intellectuals in government, and the Cartilha fills the Senate from cultural, scientific and economic organisations.

family-wage.rationale: The Cartilha and Diretrizes demand the 'family wage', and Barroso's Carta Brasileira do Trabalho says the worker must earn enough to keep his family with dignity.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Cartilha gives great weight to state-controlled cooperatives of agricultural credit so that credit reaches those who have only the capacity to produce.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Klein quotes Salgado's 1934 claim that international capitalism 'secretly foments separatist tendencies in order to weaken the nation'.

gradual-change.rationale: The Cartilha rejects partial solutions to the social question and asks for a radical revision of codes and a modification of the whole structure of the state.

harm-principle.rationale: The Diretrizes give the state supervision of cinema, theatre, press and radio for moral reasons and subordinate every individual to the superior interests of the community.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Reale wrote that 'the racist thesis' has never been part of Integralism and that in Brazil the theory of superior races shows all its weakness.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Salgado condemned Nazi sterilisation as revealing a materialist sense of life, though he also wanted a 'eugenically fit' race built on religious feeling.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Under Reale's 1934 statement reported by Klein, immigrant children would be schooled in Portuguese.

immigration-favours-shared-culture.rationale: Klein reports that A Offensiva campaigned in 1936 against Japanese immigrants as 'undesirable' because inassimilable, while the Manifesto welcomes immigrants who integrate.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Barroso's Integral State is one in which 'economic emancipation' has taken place 'as an indispensable factor of independence'.

independent-unions.rationale: The Cartilha makes the union an organ of public law under the immediate supervision and protection of the state, with only one union per category recognised.

indirect-election.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto has class representatives in the national congresses elect the Head of the Nation, those of provincial congresses the governor, and municipal chambers the mayor.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Diretrizes give the family 'intangible rights' and its own vote, and the doctrine treats natural groups such as family, corporation and municipality as bearers of rights.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The Manifesto wants a public law 'of our own, according to our realities' and blames Brazil's troubles on an inadequate imported regime.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Carta Brasileira do Trabalho gives every man a right to work, and the Manifesto-Programa makes it the state's duty to create the structures that make this right effective.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: Barroso's Carta Brasileira do Trabalho holds that capital and labour cannot exist without each other and that neither may dominate the other.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Diretrizes promise to make Christian principles respected in all the details of national legislation, which is less than law taken from scripture itself.

leader-cult.rationale: Within the movement members swore an oath of total loyalty to the Chefe Nacional (Klein), but Salgado condemned the deification of the Führer as political artificiality, so the sources point both ways.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa has the state 'proclaim the duty of work' and create the processes for its fulfilment, and the Carta calls work a social duty as well as an individual right.

limit-population.rationale: The Cartilha wants to remove the taxes that encourage birth control, 'in a land that needs many children and strong children'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Cartilha declares Integralism against free competition, which reduces labour to a commodity, and the Diretrizes put the national economy under government direction instead of the law of supply and demand.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The Diretrizes put the spiritual above the moral, social and national, and Barroso holds that only a moral, inner revolution can produce a social revolution.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: The Cartilha reserves questions of general interest to the central government alone, and Barroso wants the interstate frontiers to disappear.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Klein shows that Barroso spread theories of a Jewish world conspiracy and that Salgado and Reale echoed him, though Reale disowned racial hostility and blamed only Jews in 'international banking'.

minority-language-support.rationale: Reale told a German-Brazilian enquirer that schools would teach in Portuguese and German only as a foreign language (Klein).

moral-incentives.rationale: The Carta wants work done for an ideal 'without the exclusive concern to produce much and earn more', but the Manifesto praises the 'just ambition to progress, to own goods', so the sources point both ways.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Manifesto stands 'for religious morality' and the Diretrizes promise to make Christian principles respected in every detail of national legislation.

nation-first.rationale: The Manifesto calls cosmopolitanism a mortal evil and wants a nationalist campaign against the influence of imperialist countries, though the Manifesto-Programa also seeks South American solidarity.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Reale accepted foreign cultural associations only as long as they did not prevent 'the fusion of the German-Brazilian with the national community' (Klein).

national-mission.rationale: The Manifesto promises a 'New Civilisation' that will start from Brazil, set the continent alight and 'influence even the world'.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Manifesto promises to lift the fatherland from depression and despondency and begin a 'New Civilisation', and Barroso calls for the complete transformation of Brazil to save it.

national-resource-control.rationale: The 1935 Statutes require the use of natural resources for the benefit of the Brazilian people and the financial sovereignty of the nation, and the Cartilha nationalises mines and waterfalls.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Manifesto wants the nation directed 'by the brain of its elites', and the Cartilha understands national unity only 'according to the hierarchy of intelligence and capacity'.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto sets out to save the nation 'from the errors of capitalist civilisation and the errors of communist barbarity', and the Cartilha announces a fight without truce against both.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Cartilha requires the state to supervise and even direct the whole economy, and the Diretrizes oblige it to meet the material, intellectual and moral needs of the person.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The Diretrizes make it the state's task to keep the marriage bond indissoluble.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Diretrizes forbid the state to curtail the rights of family and religion over education and have it cooperate with them in forming new generations.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Manifesto says wealth exalts no one unless its holders fulfil the duties it strictly imposes toward society and the fatherland.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The Cartilha says government cannot be in the hands of a party or a class and can only be national, reflecting all regions and classes.

one-party-rule.rationale: Scholars describe the Integral State as ruled by a strong state and its single party, but the Diretrizes and Cartilha make all parties unnecessary in it, so the sources point both ways.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: The Manifesto declares the movement an enemy of all conspiracies and seditions and Salgado says it respects constituted authority, but he allows force once that authority collapses.

organic-representation.rationale: The Manifesto organises the nation into professional classes that elect municipal, provincial and national bodies, and the Diretrizes move the vote to corporations, natural groups and cultural associations in place of parties.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Cartilha calls for rigorous state control of press, cinema and theatre, while the Manifesto-Programa condemns government censorship and gives the press self-government as a corporation, so the sources point both ways.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Klein reports that the AIB statutes forbade members to question or criticise any decision of the national leader, on pain of expulsion.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Manifesto wants to teach young people the lesson of courage as sons of Brazil, and the Cartilha says schooling must create a national conscience before anything else.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Barroso writes that the fatherland's greatness can rest only on the working masses, freed both from stateless capitalism and from vote-hunting politicians.

pay-for-effort.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto wants the worker paid according to his needs and sharing in profits 'according to his effort and capacity'.

person-over-state.rationale: Salgado says the Integral State has no end in itself and does not subordinate the human person, whose intangibility it serves, though the Diretrizes subordinate the individual to the community.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Barroso attacks the 'regime of frauds, deceptions, corruption and empty promises', and the Manifesto says politicians conspire for personal and group interests.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The Diretrizes declare for spiritualism against materialist currents that disintegrate the nation, and Barroso says the first revolution is the inner, moral one.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Cartilha says liberty is worth nothing without a minimum of economic autonomy, and the Manifesto-Programa attacks liberalism for promising freedoms while the powerful usurp the practical means to exercise them.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Manifesto's nationalism fights cosmopolitanism, defends Brazilian traditions and customs and wants a culture and way of life 'genuinely Brazilian'.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa says press freedom needs material guarantees because financial dependence has taken most papers' freedom, and the Diretrizes say the press is forced to serve international capitalists.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The Cartilha calls for direct supervision of trade in basic necessities to stop the 'criminal activity of hoarders', and the Manifesto-Programa fights price exploitation.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Carta Brasileira do Trabalho treats capital as accumulated labour that rightly shares in the results of production, limited only so that it does not absorb all the fruits of labour.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Salgado calls the Integral State 'the state of law' and not an arbitrary one, and the Manifesto-Programa places the revolution within the frames of public and private law.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The Cartilha proposes the family wage, protected family property and the removal of taxes on the family economy because the country needs many children.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1932 Manifesto calls the right of property fundamental and natural, but the Statutes and Diretrizes defend property only up to the limit set by the common good and announce nationalisations, so the sources point both ways on how hard it is to override.

property-sabotage-justified.rationale: Barroso says Integralism does not appeal to banditry, vandalism, terrorism, dynamite or sabotage, but to the moral worth of man.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The 1935 Statutes guarantee property only 'up to the limit imposed by the common good', and the Cartilha adds that the owner has duties and answers to the state for antisocial use.

proportional-representation.rationale: The Diretrizes make parties unnecessary in the Integral State and reject representation as a quantitative expression of votes.

public-ownership.rationale: The Diretrizes promise to nationalise railways, shipping, mines, energy sources and banking, and the Cartilha lists waterfalls, banking, electricity companies, some transport and mines as forces that cannot act outside the state.

racial-franchise.rationale: Reale says the movement's ranks are open to Brazilians of every race and that it judges people by moral and civic values, not colour.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The 1935 Statutes set out to avoid struggles between races and groups of any kind and to unite all Brazilians.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The 1935 Statutes aim to avoid struggles 'between races', and the Manifesto unites all Brazilians of every region and origin in one spirit.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Cartilha says the social question is not solved by minimum-wage laws, and Klein reports that Reale dismissed the minimum wage as demagoguery; wages were to be fixed in collective contracts.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Barroso cites Maritain's lesson that reason must submit to God and to the spiritual order he instituted.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Cartilha wants taxes collected centrally and shared equitably among municipality, province and union according to national needs.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Cartilha asks for rigorous state supervision of all economic life against the control of the 'captains of industry', and the Diretrizes attack the 'orgy of trusts, cartels and monopolies' permitted by the liberal state.

religion-illusion.rationale: The Diretrizes declare Integralism spiritualist against all materialist currents, and the Manifesto opens with God directing the destinies of peoples.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: The Manifesto welcomes the children of other countries who work in Brazil and whose descendants are integrated, and Reale says honest Jews have nothing to fear.

restore-past-order.rationale: The Cartilha says Integralism respects tradition but makes it a 'landmark of continual elevation', not a point of arrival.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Cartilha sets up a labour magistracy so that disputes are settled 'without the useless sacrifice of strikes and lockouts', which it justifies only against a liberal state's indifference.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Barroso says Integralism is guided by a doctrine, not a programme, while the Cartilha says it puts 'reality above theories', so the sources point both ways.

right-to-secede.rationale: The Manifesto wants the nation 'one, indivisible' and no longer cut up by state governors, and the Statutes make national unity a core aim.

rule-by-example.rationale: Barroso says a nation is not saved with laws or states of siege but with doctrine and morals, and that the integralist revolution advances by example.

sacred-nation.rationale: Barroso says nations are bound to their past by tradition and that civilisation is a patrimony in which successive generations are united, though the Diretrizes rank the national below the spiritual, moral and social.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Salgado condemned the Nazi exaltation of the Führer to the point of deification as an artificial politics without religious basis.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Barroso treats the moral, intellectual and technical conquests of past generations as a patrimony on which the present must build.

second-chamber.rationale: The Cartilha and Barroso add a Senate drawn from cultural, scientific and spiritual professions alongside the corporative chamber.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Barroso builds national greatness on 'the renunciation of personal interests in favour of national interests', and the Manifesto says wealth exalts no one who neglects the duties it imposes.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Barroso blames the regime for enslaving Brazil to the international banker through 'heavy and successive foreign loans' and makes economic emancipation a condition of independence.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Diretrizes and Manifesto-Programa want a concordat with the Church and Christian principles applied throughout national law.

separated-powers.rationale: The Manifesto keeps the classical executive, legislative and judicial powers and the Manifesto-Programa defends the judiciary's intangibility, though the Manifesto also seeks 'the supreme authority of the nation'.

simple-living.rationale: Barroso's account of Integralism asks for the renunciation of personal interests, the simplicity of life and the modesty of conduct.

single-common-good.rationale: The Diretrizes have the state coordinate all natural groups toward the common good of the nation, and the Cartilha rejects the state as a sum of isolated individuals.

single-official-language.rationale: Klein reports Reale's 1934 statement that lessons would be in Portuguese in an integralist state, with German or Italian taught only as foreign languages.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Salgado says the Integral State is not a destroyer of the regime but the creator of new organs to revitalise it, and the Manifesto-Programa reaches power through the existing constitution.

socialized-care.rationale: The Manifesto rejects 'an absurd socialisation of affections' and keeps the family as the source of care, and the Diretrizes give it the mission of educating the child.

socialized-markets.rationale: The Diretrizes call private initiative the most fruitful factor of production and limit public ownership to a list of strategic services, so markets are not restricted to worker- or publicly-owned firms.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Salgado defines the Integral State as a state of law that is neither arbitrary nor absorbing and that strengthens itself by keeping its own limits.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The Manifesto calls communism 'Soviet capitalism' that reduces all employers to one, and Barroso calls it international capitalism disguised as state capitalism.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The Diretrizes put the spiritual above the moral, social and national, and the Manifesto-Programa says man needs an economic base even to fulfil his spiritual duties.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The Cartilha says the state is not to be confused with a class, is above the classes and can only express the whole nation.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Cartilha has the state supervise economic life, 'guiding, stimulating and even directing' it, and the Manifesto-Programa has it organise plans in particular sectors to defend national sovereignty.

state-harmful.rationale: The Diretrizes call the state the holder of sovereignty that realises the integral unity of the nation, and the Cartilha asks for a strong state.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Diretrizes commit the state to spiritualism and Christian principles, and the Manifesto condemns communism for destroying religion.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: The Cartilha makes the state 'a realiser of moral ends', and the Diretrizes commit it to the moral and spiritual improvement of the nation.

strong-leader.rationale: The Manifesto calls for an authority able to take initiatives for all, but the Cartilha says the doctrine 'flees equally from dictatorship and Caesarism', so the support is qualified.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Diretrizes and Manifesto-Programa want a concordat 'without loss of autonomy of the parties', and Salgado says the Integral State does not enter religion's own domain.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Diretrizes say the Integral State 'cannot allow' any political, social or economic force to form outside its sphere that could threaten it, and parties are abolished.

total-state.rationale: The Diretrizes say everything in the political, social and economic spheres must be controlled by the Integral State, but Salgado's 1936 summary rejects the totalitarian state that absorbs culture, economy and religion, so the sources point both ways.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Klein reports Salgado's 1933 declaration that 'only fascism' could raise Brazil again, while the movement condemned communism without truce.

traditional-family.rationale: The Manifesto calls the family 'the basis of happiness on earth' and the source of the virtues that strengthen the state, and the Diretrizes call it the first and most important social institution.

unions-good.rationale: The Cartilha calls trade unions natural, permanent bodies of the nation with political, economic, cultural and moral functions, though only within the corporative state.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Cartilha calls for free medical care in the municipalities and a national sanitary organisation run by the state.

universal-morality.rationale: Salgado says 'immutable principles' fix the limits of each person and group, and the Carta grounds property, family and association in natural law.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Manifesto-Programa holds that liberalism creates 'tyrannies of political and economic factions' that usurp the means of real liberty.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Cartilha says Integralism wants the 'dissemination of property' through popular credit rather than its destruction, and the Manifesto-Programa aims at the widest possible distribution of property as the material guarantee of the family.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The Diretrizes want the marriage bond kept indissoluble, which excludes divorce on either spouse's initiative.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The Manifesto vows to fight the ironic, the blasé and the disillusioned and to mobilise the masses, and Barroso asks each green-shirt for sacrifice for the nation.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Manifesto enrols men and women alike in professional classes, which elect the representative bodies, and Klein records women voting in the movement's internal plebiscite and training new voters.

worker-ownership.rationale: The doctrine keeps private initiative as the most fruitful factor of production and gives workers a share in profits under collective contracts, not ownership of the firms they work in.

workers-councils.rationale: Political power rests on corporations that unite employers, employees and technicians in equal conditions, alongside a senate of cultural bodies, not on councils of workers.

workers-nation.rationale: The Manifesto rallies workers to national unity against internationalist communism, and the Cartilha accepts internationalism only as a result of the specific values of each nation.

workers-own-party.rationale: The doctrine abolishes political parties and has workers represented through their unions and corporations instead.

missingStatements.text: The family, not the individual, should be the basic unit of political representation.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto's chapters on the family and the municipality as the nation's cell, and the aim of organizing powers around families, municipalities and producing classes, place the family at the base of the state.

missingStatements.text: A nation's unity should be based on a shared spiritual identity rather than on race.
missingStatements.rationale: Salgado defined nationalism as a spiritual identity of a heterogeneous nation, with the slogan union of all races and peoples.

notes: Later pass (rules 5) by claude-opus-5-5. The first pass rested on Wikipedia and an excerpt of the Manifesto; this pass read the full October 1932 Manifesto, the Statutes, Diretrizes, Cartilha and 1936 Manifesto-Programa, and 1934-37 texts by Salgado, Reale and Barroso (archived copies from the Frente Integralista Brasileira site, read through the Wayback Machine because the live site's certificate chain does not verify), plus Klein's CEDLA monograph and Lesser's encyclopedia entry. Every first-pass answer was rechecked; those the sources do not settle are nulled. The AIB never governed, so answers rest on its words; its 1938 putsch and paramilitary militia are not counted as an ideology's record. The Diretrizes copy is a later edition, and the Cartilha copy folds in Reale's 1936 revisions. Barroso's antisemitic books (e.g. Brasil, colônia de banqueiros) were not available; the antisemitic strand is answered from Klein and Reale. Themes searched: economy (property, corporations, unions, wages, nationalisation, credit, planning), government (representation, parties, federalism, head of state, rule of law), society (family, divorce, religion, education, race, immigration, women), world (South American unity, foreign capital, communism, fascism) and means (revolution, force, legality). Ecology, technology and most world questions (alliances, the UN, war) stay null: the sources say nothing on them. Postwar PRP texts on the same archive were not used.
